opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it came down to wanting something that felt approachable. The work we do sits at the intersection of AI and drug discovery, and both of those fields can get really jargon-heavy and intimidating. We didn't want a name that sounded like a pharma conglomerate or some invented tech word with too many consonants. We wanted something short and easy to say that people would remember after hearing it once.

Chai has that warmth to it. It's something people share, something you sit down with. That fit how we think about the company. We're trying to build tools that scientists actually want to use, that feel like a collaborator rather than a black box. A simple name signals that we're about making hard things more accessible, not adding complexity.

There's also a practical side. When you're a small team trying to recruit great people and get your models into researchers' hands, every bit of friction matters. If someone hears the name at a conference or reads it in a paper, you want them to be able to find you, spell it, and talk about it with their colleagues without thinking twice. Simple names travel well.

And I think there's a bit of a philosophy in it too. The underlying science is incredibly complex: predicting molecular structures, understanding how proteins interact, designing new therapeutics. But the goal is simple: help bring better medicines to patients faster. We wanted the name to reflect that clarity of purpose rather than the complexity of the method.

r001.rationale: The response links the simple name to making difficult work more accessible and says the company aims to avoid adding complexity, expressing a broader goal of making biotechnology easier to engage with.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came from a pretty simple place. We spent a lot of time thinking about what we wanted to build, and almost no time thinking about the name, which I think is actually the right order.

The thing I kept coming back to is that so many biotech and AI companies have these names that are trying very hard. They've got a Greek root, or a clever portmanteau, or some reference to a protein that only people in the field will catch. And every time you say it out loud you have to spell it, and then you have to explain it. That's friction, and it compounds. You're saying your company's name thousands of times, in pitches, in recruiting, in papers, in casual conversation.

Chai is a word people already know. It's warm, it's short, it's easy to say in any language, and people tend to smile a little when they hear it. That was kind of the whole bar. I didn't want a name that signaled how smart we were. I wanted a name that got out of the way so the work could be the thing people remembered.

There's also a slightly deeper version of it, which is that we're trying to make molecular design feel approachable. The science underneath is incredibly complicated, but the experience of using what we build shouldn't feel that way. A simple, friendly name is a small way of making that promise up front.

And honestly, a bunch of us just drink a lot of chai. That was probably eighty percent of it. The rest is me rationalizing after the fact.

r001.rationale: The response connects the friendly name to making molecular design approachable, saying the complicated science should be easier to experience. This communicates the broader aim of making biotechnology simpler.

astra-6.text: We wanted a name that was short, memorable, and easy to say. Biology is already complicated; the company’s name doesn’t need to be. Chai felt warm and approachable, and we liked that.

r001.rationale: The response explains the name’s simplicity as a way to keep the company approachable because biology is complicated, but it does not connect that choice to a broader aim of making biotechnology simpler.
